source_text:
Quanto uerius de diis uestris animalia muta naturaliter iudicant! mures, hirundines, milui non sentire eos sciunt: rodunt, inculcant, insident, ac nisi abigatis, in ipso dei uestri ore nidificant: araneae uero faciem eius intexunt et de ipso capite sua fila suspendunt.
uos tergetis, mundatis, eraditis et illos, quos facitis protegitis, et timetis, dum unusquisque uestrum non cogitat prius se debere deum nosse quam colere, dum inconsulte gestiunt parentibus oboedire, dum fieri malunt alieni erroris accessio quam sibi credere, dum nihil ex his quae timent norunt. sic in auro et argento auaritia consecrata est, sic statuarum inanium consignata forma, sic nata Romana superstitio: quorum ritus si percenseas, ridenda quam multa, quam multa etiam miseranda sunt !
nudi cruda hieme discurrunt, alii incedunt pilleati, scuta uetera circumferunt, pelles caedunt, mendicantes uicatim deos ducunt: quaedam fana semel anno adire permittunt, quaedam in totum nefas uisere: est quo uiro non licet, nonnulla absque feminis sacra sunt, etiam seruo quibusdam caerimoniis interesse piaculare flagitium est: alia sacra coronat uniuira, alia multiuira, et magna religione conquiritur quae plura possit adulteria numerare.
quid, qui sanguine suo libat et uulneribus suis supplicat, non profanus melius esset quam sic religiosus? aut cui testa sunt obscena demessa, quo modo deum non uiolat qui hoc modo placat, cum si eunuchos deus uellet, posset procreare, non facere? quis non intellegat male sanos et uanae et perditae mentis in ista desipere et ipsam errantium turbam mutua sibi patrocinia praestare? hic defensio communis furoris est furentium multitudo.
thought_title: The gods are judged by animals and their rites are absurd
orientation: Octavius is continuing his attack on the pagan gods, now arguing that even animals treat the idols as lifeless matter and that the rites of Roman worship are ridiculous or shameful.
pass_a_gloss: How much more truly do mute animals judge naturally about your gods! Mice, swallows, kites know that they do not feel: they gnaw, trample, sit on them, and unless you drive them away, they build nests in the very mouth of your god: spiders indeed weave over his face and hang their threads from his very head. You wipe, clean, scrape them and protect those whom you make, and you fear them, while each one of you does not think that he ought first to know God than to worship him, while they rashly desire to obey their parents, while they prefer to become an addition to another's error than to believe themselves, while they know nothing of those things which they fear. Thus in gold and silver greed has been consecrated, thus the form of empty statues has been sealed, thus Roman superstition was born: if you review their rites, how many things are laughable, how many things are also pitiable! Naked they run about in raw winter, others walk wearing felt caps, they carry around old shields, they beat hides, begging they lead gods through the villages: some shrines they permit to be approached once a year, some it is a sin to visit at all: there is a place where a man is not allowed, some rites are without women, even for a slave to be present at certain ceremonies is an expiatory crime: some rites a one-man woman crowns, others a many-man woman, and with great religion a woman is sought who can count more adulteries. What of the one who pours a libation with his own blood and prays with his own wounds, would he not be better as profane than as religious in this way? Or the one whose obscene parts are cut off, how does he not violate God who pleases him in this way, since if God wanted eunuchs, he could create them, not make them? Who would not understand that the unsound and those of empty and ruined mind are mad in these things and that the very crowd of the erring gives mutual patronage to itself? Here the defense of common madness is the multitude of the raging.

choices.why: Keeps the literal contrast between speechless animals and the supposedly speaking gods; 'mute' preserves the adjective's force.

choices.term: in ipso dei uestri ore nidificant
choices.english: build nests in the very mouth of your god
choices.why: Literal rendering of 'ore' as 'mouth' preserves the shocking image of birds nesting in the idol's face.
rejected: in the very face of your god

choices.why: Literal calques preserve the Latin compounds' structure and the contrast between a woman married once and one with many husbands.
rejected: woman married once / woman married many times

choices.why: Literal rendering of 'accessio' as 'addition' keeps the metaphor of people appending themselves to inherited false belief.

choices.term: male sanos et uanae et perditae mentis
choices.english: the unsound and those of empty and ruined mind
choices.why: Literal rendering of the genitive of quality 'uanae et perditae mentis' preserves the double description of mental state.
rejected: the insane and those of vain and ruined mind
the mentally ill and those of empty and lost mind

choices.why: Literal rendering of 'patrocinia praestare' as 'gives patronage' preserves the legal metaphor of defense.

pass_b_english: How much more truly do mute animals judge your gods by nature! Mice, swallows, and kites know that the gods feel nothing: they gnaw them, trample them, sit on them, and unless you drive them away, they build nests in the very mouth of your god. Spiders weave over his face and hang their threads from his very head.

You wipe them, clean them, scrape them, and you protect the gods you make, and you fear them—while each of you does not think that he ought to know God before he worships him, while you are eager to obey your parents without thought, while you prefer to become an addition to another's error rather than trust yourselves, while you know nothing of the things you fear. So greed has been consecrated in gold and silver, so the form of empty statues has been sealed, so Roman superstition was born. If you review their rites, how many are laughable, how many are also pitiable!

Some run about naked in the raw winter, others walk wearing felt caps, carry old shields around, beat hides, and lead gods begging through the streets. Some shrines they allow to be entered once a year, some it is forbidden to visit at all. There is one where no man may go, some rites are closed to women, and for a slave even to be present at certain ceremonies is a crime requiring expiation. Other rites a one-husband woman crowns, others a many-husband woman, and with great religiosity the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out.

What of the man who pours a libation with his own blood and prays with his own wounds? Would he not be better off profane than religious in this way? Or the man whose testicles are cut off—how does he not violate the god whom he placates in this manner, since if God wanted eunuchs, he could create them, not make them? Who does not understand that the unsound and those of empty and ruined mind are raving in these practices, and that the crowd of the erring itself offers mutual defense to one another? Here the common defense of madness is the multitude of the mad.

problems.why: Latin means a shameful/flagitious crime, not expiatory
'testa' = testicles; euphemistic but clear; 'obscena' = shameful/private parts; 'demessa' = cut off; should be more direct or use proper anatomical reference
problems.fix: whose testicles are cut off, his shameful parts removed
problems.ruling: testa = testicles; translation vague loses specific anatomy

problems.why: 'patrocinia praestare' = offer mutual defense/protection; 'patronage' in modern English suggests client-patron relationship, not the legal defense meant
problems.fix: offers mutual defense to one another
problems.ruling: mutua sibi patrocinia praestare = give each other mutual patronage, not self‑patronage

problems.why: Latin refers to rites crowned by a single woman and by many women; translation is nonsensical
problems.fix: a rite crowned by a single woman, another by many women
problems.ruling: 'uniuira' means married to one man, 'multiuira' to many; translation 'one-man woman' inverts meaning to woman's husbands, not rite's participants.

edits.old: whose obscene parts are cut away

edits.new: offers mutual defense to one another

edits.old: Some rites are crowned by a one-man woman, others by a many-man woman
edits.new: Some rites are crowned by a woman who has had one husband, others by a woman who has had many

fixed: Changed 'expiatory crime' to 'shameful crime': 'piaculare flagitium' means a shameful/flagitious crime, not expiatory.
Changed 'obscene parts are cut away' to 'testicles are cut off': 'testa' means testicles, 'demessa' means cut off.
Changed 'gives mutual patronage to itself' to 'offers mutual defense to one another': 'patrocinia praestare' means to offer defense/protection, not patronage.
Changed 'one-man woman'/'many-man woman' to 'woman who has had one husband'/'woman who has had many': 'uniuira' and 'multiuira' refer to a woman married once or many times.

problems.why: Latin 'inculcant' means 'bite' or 'gnaw', not 'trample'; the English misstates the action.

problems.quote: while you eagerly obey your parents without reflection
problems.why: 'gestiunt' means 'are eager/long,' but 'inconsulte' modifies the eagerness; 'without reflection' applies to the eagerness, not separate obedience
problems.fix: while they are eager to obey their parents without thought
problems.ruling: 'gestiunt' = they practice/obey, not 'eagerly'; translation adds unwarranted sense of eagerness.

problems.quote: Some rites are crowned by a woman who has had one husband
problems.why: 'coronat' is active: 'a woman who has had one husband crowns/crowns over other rites,' not passive 'are crowned'
problems.fix: Other rites a one-husband woman crowns
problems.ruling: 'coronat' active; translation passive 'are crowned' changes agency.

problems.quote: with great religion they seek out the woman who can count the most adulteries
problems.source_quote: et magna religione conquiritur quae plura possit adulteria numerare
problems.why: 'conquiritur' is passive 'is sought out,' not active 'they seek out'; and 'magna religione' is ablative of manner
problems.fix: and with great religious scruple the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out
problems.ruling: 'conquiritur' passive; English active 'they seek out' misrepresents voice.

edits.old: they gnaw them, trample them, sit on them
edits.new: they gnaw them, bite them, sit on them

edits.old: while you eagerly obey your parents without reflection
edits.new: while you are eager to obey your parents without thought

edits.old: Some rites are crowned by a woman who has had one husband, others by a woman who has had many
edits.new: Other rites a one-husband woman crowns, others a many-husband woman

edits.old: and with great religion they seek out the woman who can count the most adulteries
edits.new: and with great religious scruple the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out

fixed: inculcant means 'bite' or 'gnaw', not 'trample'; changed to 'bite them'.
dum inconsulte gestiunt parentibus oboedire: 'inconsulte' modifies the eagerness; changed to 'while you are eager to obey your parents without thought'.
alia sacra coronat uniuira: 'coronat' is active, not passive; changed to 'Other rites a one-husband woman crowns, others a many-husband woman'.
conquiritur is passive 'is sought out', not active 'they seek out'; changed to 'the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out'.

problems.quote: with great religious scruple the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out
problems.source_quote: et magna religione conquiritur quae plura possit adulteria numerare
problems.why: Latin "magna religione" means "with great religiosity/reverence", not "scruple" (moral hesitation). The English adds a wrong nuance.
problems.fix: and with great religiosity the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out

problems.why: inculcant means tread/trample, not bite; animals walk on idols
non cogitat means 'does not think,' not 'never thinks'; simple negation, not temporal
problems.ruling: non cogitat = does not think, not 'never thinks'

problems.why: ironic: 'with great religious scruple' misses sarcasm; 'with great ceremony/religious show' better
problems.ruling: magna religione = great ceremony/religion, not 'religious scruple'

edits.old: they gnaw them, bite them, sit on them
edits.new: they gnaw them, trample them, sit on them

edits.old: while each of you never thinks
edits.new: while each of you does not think

edits.old: with great religious scruple the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out
edits.new: with great religiosity the woman who can count more adulteries is sought out

fixed: bite them -> trample them: source 'inculcant' means trample, not bite.
never thinks -> does not think: source 'non cogitat' is simple negation, not temporal.
with great religious scruple -> with great religiosity: source 'magna religione' means great religiosity/reverence, not scruple.

fixed.quote: know that they have no feeling
fixed.fix: know that the gods feel nothing
fixed.note: In English, 'they' most naturally points back to the animals, but the Latin says the gods lack feeling; the proposed fix keeps the same unclear 'they'.
Piaculare means the act needs ritual expiation, which 'shameful' does not say; the proposed fix would produce 'an an expiatory crime' after the existing 'a'.

dismissed.why: Lowercase 'God' here refers to pagan gods generally, not the Christian God; context is pagan worship.
dismissed.note: Octavius states a general principle that one must know God before worshipping him, and the capital is standard (compare ANF).
